p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Telemedicine promised to carry the specialist to the village. A patient in a remote taluka can now consult a doctor in a city hospital through a video call, share reports instantly and receive a digital prescription. During the pandemic such services kept routine care going when clinics were closed, and government platforms recorded millions of consultations. Yet the technology cannot examine an abdomen or listen to a chest; it depends on a trained health worker at the patient's end and on a reliable internet connection that many villages still lack. Older and less literate patients often find the process confusing, and doctors worry about missing signs that a physical examination would reveal. Telemedicine is therefore best seen not as a substitute for the local clinic but as an extension of it, most useful for follow-up visits, specialist opinions and the management of chronic illness.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Leadership is commonly pictured as an act of speaking: the general rallying troops, the chief executive announcing a strategy, the captain urging a tired team towards one last effort. These scenes are real, but they show only the visible half of the work. The less dramatic half consists of listening, and it is here that many capable leaders fail. Promotion tends to reward those who have answers, and by the time a person reaches the top of an organisation, the habit of supplying answers may have crowded out the habit of asking questions. Subordinates soon learn what the leader wishes to hear and begin to supply it.

Genuine listening is harder than it looks because it requires a leader to tolerate being contradicted, sometimes in public, by people of lower rank. It requires patience with hesitant speakers, who are often the ones closest to the problem, and a willingness to delay a decision until the relevant voices have been heard. Leaders who manage this gain more than information. They earn the confidence of people who feel their knowledge has been taken seriously, and that confidence becomes a reserve on which the organisation can draw in difficult times. A leader who only speaks may be obeyed; a leader who also listens is more likely to be followed.
